title: EGY-17 · The Egyptian media: podcasts, documentaries, transcription and subtitles

blocks.text: EGY-17 · The Egyptian media: podcasts, documentaries,
transcription and subtitles
Lesson overview

The talk of the media is the richest source of authentic Egyptian: podcasts, documentaries, long interviews, popular videos. Compared to the dialogues of the course is faster, more disordered (pauses, repetitions, self-corrections, sentences left in half) and more mixed: English words in the podcasts of young people, fuṣḥā in the voice of the narrator and in the vocabulary of experts. In this unit learn the discursive signals that organize a story or reasoning, the rapid forms of quick speech, the conventions to transcribe the Egyptian into Arabic characters and the techniques to translate it into English, both in an integral translation and in subtitles. It's the Egyptian side of the translation form. Eight weeks, in parallel with the end of B2-13, B2-14 and B2-15.

rows: EGY-11 EGY-16 (in particular EGY-14, interviews, and EGY-16, the graphs); B2-13 in parallel
12–13 hours · eight weeks (weeks) 211–218), about 1,5 hours per week in two blocks

blocks.text: Materials This unit, an Egyptian tutor, podcasts and authentic Egyptian videos chosen by the tutor, a program to slow down audio
Targets. At the end of the unit you know:
1. follow 10–15 minutes of a podcast or an interview in Egyptian, understanding the main points and details
important;
2. recognize the discursive signals of the story and reasoning and their function;
3. understand the most frequent rapid forms of fast speech and adapted English words;
4. transcribe into Arabic characters one minute of Egyptian, faithful version and clean version;
5. translate the Egyptian spoken in English, in full version and in subtitles.
Eight-week plan (two blocks from 40–45 minutes per week).

rows: Oral and written production 1–3 with the tutor

2. The Discursive Signs
In EGY-11 and EGY-14 you learned buṣṣ, aṣl, ʿala fikra, il-muhimm, ʾaṣdi. Podcasts and long interviews use many more: they organize the speech as the connectives organize an article.

blocks.text: biyʾullak. Lett. "He says to you": in reality, there is no one speaking to you. It is used to report a news heard, often with some irony or doubt: biyʾullak il-banzīn hayġla tāni It seems that petrol is increasing again. In translation: "Pare che" , "Sacco che"; not ... tell you.
3. The quick talk
Words melt in the quick talk. The most frequent forms:
ʾāl lu ʾallu He told him

The English words. In youth podcasts and work videos, English words are frequent, with Egyptian grammar: the article i- (the-kontentbōstāt (Posted) and especially the verb ʿamal "Do" + English: ʿamal šēr "She shared" ʿamal lāyk "I like it" haniʿmil lāyv We'll do a direct . In translation, the current Italian word (share, contents) is used, not English.
4. Transcribe
Transcribe ( ⁧تفريغ⁩ , tafrīġ) means writing down an audio. It is often a job for those who know Arabic, and the first step of each translation of an audio. Two types of transcription.

rows: Everything: hesitations ( ⁧إمم، آه⁩ ), repetitions, interrupted sentences, self-corrections, laughter
precise analysis of what has been said and how
the words of the speaker without hesitation or unnecessary repetition; Egyptian grammar remains

blocks.text: Conventional signs.
Initial speaker or role + two points ( ⁧ضيف⁩ ) ⁧ض:⁩ · ( ⁧مذيعة⁩ ) ⁧م:⁩

The graphs. Use the consistent graphs of EGY-16 ( ⁧أوي، ده، عايز، دلوقتي، هـ⁩ for the future). English words are written in the most common Arabic spelling ( ⁧أوكي، الكونتنت⁩ ). The qāf pronounced as hamza (ʾ) is written ⁧ق⁩ : ʾāl → ⁧قال⁩ . The method. 1) Listen to everything once without writing. 2) Divide audio into pieces of 10–15 seconds. 3) Write each piece, leaving empty spaces where you don't understand. 4) Listen only to empty spaces, even at reduced speed. 5) Read everything while you listen again. 6) If you can, have an Egyptian speaker check out the uncertain words. At the beginning one minute of audio requires 20–30 working minutes: it's normal.
5. Pronunciation

The rhythm of the story. Those who tell in a podcast use the voice: elongates vowels for emphasis (kbīīīr Very large; wallāāāhi), slow down before the surprise (laʾ w-ēh...) and accelerates in the least important parts. Shadowing exercise: choose 30 Seconds of Script B, listen to a sentence and repeat it immediately above the reader's voice, imitating rhythm and intonation, as long as you can follow it without stopping.

7. Documentaries and news: three entries

rows: Egyptian grammar ( ⁧ده، مش، بـ، هـ⁩ ) with vocabulary of fuṣḥā

blocks.text: people interviewed for Egyptian fast pace, discursive signals, Italian proverbs spoken simple, daily street without dialect

The educated Egyptian. The educated people, when they talk about technical or public subjects, use Egyptian grammar with many words of fuṣḥā, spoken to the Egyptian ( ⁧ث⁩ → s/t, ⁧ذ⁩ → z/d, ⁧ق⁩ → ʾ, but often q in the words translated): il-qawāʿid, il-mawḍūʿ from miḥtāg dirāsa. Sometimes they pass to the fuṣḥā full for a quotation, a figure or a solemn conclusion. You will study this switch in B2-17; Just recognize her here.
8. Translate the speech and sub-owner

Full translation (for a dossier, a translated transcription, a quote): faithful to the content; hesitations and repetitions without meaning are removed (B2-14); the signs that bear meaning are retained (but huwwa → is that they are not; laʾ w-ēh → is not finished (). In square brackets, the useful phenomena ([laughs], [incomprehensible]) are indicated. Subtitles have their own rules, because the viewer has to read while he looks at:

rows: at most two lines, approximately 40 characters per line
from one to six seconds per subtitle
a unit of meaning per subtitle; hesitations, repetitions, discursive signals are cut off
names, numbers, denials, degree of certainty
